system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2143-10-17 20:22:00 to 2143-10-22 17:06:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of orthotopic liver transplant, chronic kidney disease, gastrostomy dependence, and chronic lower extremity edema, was admitted for worsening left leg swelling and erythema following a blister rupture, concerning for cellulitis. He was initially treated with IV vancomycin and evaluated for deep vein thrombosis, which was ruled out by Doppler ultrasound. The patient showed clinical improvement, with reduced edema and erythema, and was transitioned to oral cephalexin and sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim for a ten-day course. Wound care was optimized, and he was advised to hold topical clobetasol during antibiotic treatment. His kidney function remained stable, and he was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up plans and instructions for leg elevation and future use of compression therapy.
problems: Cellulitis and abscess of leg, except foot
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of large intestine

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been really sick for about a week—nausea, vomiting, and constant diarrhea. I can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, chills, or blood in your stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or blood. But I haven’t been able to take my meds either. It all started after my apartment flooded last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be a trigger. We’ll run some tests. Your labs show your kidneys are under stress—your creatinine is 2.7, up from your baseline of 1.4.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s not good. Is it from not drinking enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. We also found you’re retaining urine. Your bladder’s full, and that’s backing up on your kidneys. We’ll place a catheter to help drain it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I guess that makes sense. Will that fix my kidney numbers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll give you IV fluids too. Most of your kidney function should recover once we fix the dehydration and empty your bladder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about the nausea? I haven’t been able to eat or drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking for infections—stool tests, blood work. So far, nothing serious like C. diff or salmonella. We gave you Zofran in the ER for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had chronic diarrhea for years. I take opium tincture and loperamide. Could this be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but the sudden worsening suggests something new. We’ll keep monitoring. For now, we’re holding your tube feeds to rest your gut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But I need nutrition. I’m already thin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. We’ll restart your tube feeds once your symptoms stabilize. You’re also on your regular meds, except we stopped losartan because your blood pressure’s been low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my transplant meds—MMF and prednisone—are they safe to keep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing those. Hepatology agrees. We also checked your CMV—it’s negative, so no infection there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your ultrasound yesterday showed your liver transplant is healthy—no blockages or fluid. Bile ducts are a bit dilated, but unchanged from before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my bladder? Is the catheter helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your kidney function is already improving—BUN dropped from 67 to 40. We’ll keep the catheter in today and try removing it tomorrow if you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m still nauseous, though. Any idea why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still unclear. We tested for norovirus and other bugs—nothing positive. Since your chronic diarrhea hasn’t improved with meds, we’d like to do a flexible sigmoidoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather not. I’ve had enough procedures. Is it really necessary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not urgent, but it could help find the cause of your long-term diarrhea. We’ll respect your decision. For now, we’ll focus on symptom control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney numbers keep improving—creatinine is now 2.0. We did another bladder ultrasound. Prostate looks normal, no blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So can we remove the catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll do a void trial today. You’ll try to urinate on your own, and we’ll check how much is left in your bladder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You passed the void trial! Bladder scan shows only a small amount left. We’ll remove the catheter and monitor you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a huge relief. I hate catheters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We do too. Just keep us posted if you have trouble urinating again. We still recommend urology follow-up in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nausea has improved, and you’ve been tolerating small sips. We’re restarting your tube feeds today at a low rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m worried about losing more weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. You’re still malnourished, but this is a step forward. We’ll increase feeds slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my heart? I have long QT. Should I be worried with all these changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We’ve been watching your electrolytes. Your potassium and magnesium are stable. We’ll check them again before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your creatinine is down to 1.7, back to your baseline. Your nausea is much better, and you’re keeping down oral intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll make sure your tube feeds are running well and confirm your meds are set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another procedure later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We still recommend a colonoscopy as an outpatient to check for causes of chronic diarrhea, but it’s your choice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll think about it. What else should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Watch for nausea, vomiting, or trouble urinating. Check your blood pressure regularly—losartan is on hold for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? I’ve been using Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll continue OxyContin and Dilaudid as needed. Same with your lidocaine patches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your labs are stable, you’re eating and urinating fine, and your tube feeds are running.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need urology in two weeks. Also, check potassium and magnesium at your next PCP visit due to your heart condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my daughter will help with the tube feeds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, home care will set that up. Take all your meds as listed, and call if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of liver transplant, chronic kidney disease, and chronic diarrhea, was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea following a home flood. He was found to have acute kidney injury due to hypovolemia and urinary retention. A catheter was placed, and IV fluids were given, leading to improvement in renal function by hospital day 2. His nausea persisted, but infectious workup was negative, and he gradually tolerated oral intake. Tube feeds were restarted and advanced. He refused a planned flexible sigmoidoscopy but was able to maintain nutrition. He passed a void trial and was discharged home with stable kidney function, instructions to resume tube feeds, and recommendations for urology and PCP follow-up, including electrolyte monitoring due to prolonged QT syndrome.
